title: Your own holy days
hook: anniversaries, births, deaths, turning points: Smyrna kept its bishop's death day as his birthday
tomorrow: Seneca visited his old house and didn't know his own trees. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: eight nights. Hillel's rule: one more light each night, because in holy things you go up. Today, the days on your own calendar.

A phone remembers birthdays for you. It has no field for the day someone died, the day you left, the day everything turned. A church in the old city of Smyrna once kept a different kind of calendar. Their bishop, Polycarp, was an old man when the authorities ordered him to curse Christ. He refused, and he was killed in the stadium. So why, a letter from that church says, did they plan to keep the day of his death with gladness, and call it a birthday?
screen: `THE PHONE KEEPS BIRTHDAYS.` → `POLYCARP REFUSES TO CURSE.` → `A DEATH DAY CALLED A BIRTHDAY?`

segments.voice: The letter tells what they did next. They gathered his bones, dearer to them than precious stones, and laid them in a fitting place. And they planned to meet there, in gladness, to keep the birthday of his martyrdom. Birthday: the day his life was finished and, as they believed, began. From days like this one grew a Christian custom: keeping a saint's feast on the day they died, their birthday into heaven, in Latin dies natalis. That's why, on the church calendar, a saint's day can be a death day. Inside the tradition, people argued over birthdays. The scholar Origen noticed that the only birthday parties he could find in scripture belong to Pharaoh and to Herod, and both ended with someone put to death. Ecclesiastes seems to lean his way: a good name is better than precious ointment, it says, "and the day of death than the day of one's birth." The other side has the angel, promising that at John the Baptist's coming "many shall rejoice at his birth." And the church kept that too: John's birth has its own feast. So the calendar holds both. A death can be kept as a birthday, and a birth can be holy. What the calendar won't do is let the days that made a life pass by unmarked. Births, deaths, the day you moved, the day you got well: a life has its own feast days, if someone keeps them.
screen: `BONES DEARER THAN PRECIOUS STONES.` · `HIS DEATH DAY KEPT AS A BIRTHDAY.` · `ORIGEN: ONLY PHARAOH AND HEROD.` · `THE ANGEL: MANY SHALL REJOICE.` · then, large: `MY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Open your calendar, or a blank page. Write down three days that are holy to you: a birth, a death, a turning point. Then give each one its own stretch of the sit, one at a time, in quiet.
Your own holy days: the births, deaths and turning points you choose to mark, the way Smyrna marked Polycarp's day.
Your line: my days. Smyrna kept a death day as a birthday, and the church kept John's birth too. Day 1641, marked.

howItsDone: The church calendar keeps saints' feasts, often on the day they died, and a few births, like John the Baptist's. Families also keep their own days: anniversaries of a death, a wedding, a birth.

Smyrna.meaning: an ancient city on the Aegean coast, today's Izmir

Polycarp.meaning: the bishop of Smyrna, put to death for refusing to curse Christ

dies natalis.meaning: Latin for birthday; a saint's day of death

Origen.meaning: an early Christian scholar and teacher from Alexandria

Herod.meaning: the ruler whose birthday feast ended with John the Baptist's death
